Q116243170.summary: Along this long marble lid a young shepherd, Christ, stands at the centre between two flocks: sheep crowd in from the left under leafy trees, and goats press in from the right, framed by fluted shell-like ornaments at each end. Carved for a Christian burial, it gives quiet form to Christ's words about the Last Judgement, when the Son of Man will separate the sheep from the goats.
facts: The lid is about 2.37 m long and weighs about 103 kg; the Met acquired it through the Rogers Fund in 1924.
Early Christian art often expressed the Last Judgement through Christ's parable of the sheep and the goats, long before the later type of Christ enthroned as judge became common.
Q116243170.notes: The Met's date carries a question mark: 'late 3rd–early 4th century (?)'.

walters:71.158.summary: In the central panel of this small ivory triptych the Virgin holds the Christ Child on her left arm and points to him with her right hand; the Child, with a cross-nimbus, blesses and holds a scroll. Beneath a pierced arch, mother and Son face the viewer, while on the wings two pairs of saints, one above the other, turn to them in homage. Traces of pigment and gold show that it was once brightly painted.
facts: The Virgin's pose is the Hodegetria, named after a famous icon in the Hodegon monastery in Constantinople that was believed in the Middle Ages to have been painted by St Luke.
The Walters notes that the panels were cut down and do not align perfectly, so the triptych may have been assembled from two earlier pieces.
It was once given by Bishop Heinrich von Hofstätter of Passau to the Gnadenkapelle at Altötting in Bavaria (1867).
